body:
Thanks for the report! I took a look at your code and it seems like the documentation is not very clear about this.

When you define a property path using slashes like in your demo, it creates subgroups within the current group context. For example, creating a property with the name "hello_son/hi_data/uh..." would create the desired nesting that you described.

However, when you create a group like you did with the `PROPERTY_USAGE_GROUP`, this moves the current group context down; now the "hello_son" subgroup that you were mentioning doesn't exist in the context, and so it creates a new group underneath the currently created group. This leads to the repeated groups that you noticed.

That being said, only properties and subgroups are affected by this change in context, so if you created a new group it would have to be relative to the highest layer.

There are couple of options if you wanted to have that organization:

Option 1:
Delete the prefix of the second property "uh...". This can be a bit undesirable as it separates the name of the property from the group.

Option 2:
Use a hint_string: Add a line like `"hint_string": "hello_son_hi_dad_"` to the group property. This tells the editor that any property starting with that string is a part of the group. Then, you would name the second property "hello_son_hi_dad_uh...", making sure that it has the prefix of the hint_string. This is how the editor creates properties internally for the most part.

Note that if you want a group within another group you should use the `PROPERTY_USAGE_SUBGROUP` hint.

Option 3:
Define the property as "hello_son/hi_dad/uh..." and omit the group declaration. This is fine for one property but may become cumbersome for multiple.

Option 4:
After a bit of experimentation, I think this is the most flexible approach.
Create a bunch of groups with the indentation that you want like "Hello Son/Hi Dad" or "Hello Son", and then add the related properties directly after the group that it should be in, using the "hint_string" prefixes like "hello_son_enabled" (assuming the "Hello Son" group has the "hello_son_" hint string). This allows for arbitrary indentation while still being clear about what each variable means.

Thanks very much for the help. Option 2 was the most helpful, as it seemed to fit my specific use case perfectly, being very easy to implement. I've been doing a lot of weird stuff with property lists lately, so the information you've outlined here is particularly helpful. So again, thanks for the help.

![Fixed, and also slightly updated, inspector output.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dfa58b87-54f4-4a43-908c-e8e3f6596564)
Just curious, was there anything missing in the `@export` annotation that made you use the custom property lists feature?

I'm updating my PaperSkeleton addon, which lets Godot's 2D skeletal rigs be natively rendered in 3D by making a 3D equivalent that mimics the original. This addon dynamically makes shader materials for each generated mesh instance to make sure that they mimic their equivalent Polygon2Ds.

Anyway, this addon has custom shader support, of which is why I needed to have property lists for this sort of thing. I wanted shader uniforms to be editable within the inspector, which required me to fetch each shader's uniform list, and format them into a more displayable format to fit in the inspector. The main hitch I've had to deal with regarding that is I had to make my own custom shader uniform parser, as Godot annoyingly doesn't natively expose a shader uniform's default value.

The screenshots in my previous posts are me updating it to display uniform grouping, of which I feel rather dumb for not knowing were a native feature until recently, especially since I already implemented my own hacky arbitrary system for that (which is being removed in the next release for obvious reasons).
